title: I Gave Two Boys Different Consequences for the Same Fight
author: Larry J. Walsh
summary: Larry J. Walsh narrates, as a principal, a single week in which two ninth graders who fought received different consequences. Investigation showed that one boy had been robbed of lunch money since September, had reported it to a teacher in October, and that the report had fallen between two offices. The principal suspended the aggressor for three days and gave the victim a day of in-school reflection, a restorative conversation and a parent meeting, over the objection of his assistant principal, who wanted the code of conduct applied uniformly. Both families came in angry, one because the outcome looked unfair and the other because the school had failed their son. Walsh draws the principle that consistent discipline means applying the same reasoning to every student rather than the same penalty, and that context-based fairness cannot always be explained because privacy protects every file. He also describes the system fix, a single intake log for peer-harm reports.
points: Same punishment is not the same as fair treatment: the article argues consistency lies in applying one standard of reasoning to every case.
The real failure was institutional, since an October bullying report vanished between a teacher and the counselor for four months, and the fix was one shared intake log checked weekly.
Privacy law means leaders often cannot explain a decision to the family who feels wronged, so reasoning should be written down before anyone asks.
Owning adult failures without excusing the student's own choices lets a leader tell a parent they are right and still refuse to erase a record.
Honest disagreement within the leadership team, here between the assistant principal's code-of-conduct view and the counselor's restorative view, is left unresolved rather than tidied up.
quotes: Fairness and sameness are often different things, and families can feel the difference first.
The report had fallen into the gap between two offices. For four months.
I could not tell her about the other boy’s discipline. Privacy law does not bend for fairness.
We built a single intake log for every peer-harm report that fall. Every teacher, every counselor, one form, one place.
I think a code of conduct that cannot see what happened in September is a code of conduct that punishes the kid who finally stopped waiting for us.
Consistent discipline means applying the same reasoning to every student, not handing every student the same consequence regardless of what the investigation finds.
The harder part is that fairness built on context is fairness you cannot fully explain, because privacy protects every student in the file.
So write your reasoning down before anyone asks for it, own the adult failures without excusing the student’s choices, and accept that some families will leave your office believing you were unfair.
